influence of the ninth of Moore’s ‘Odes to Nea’ (1806) is less speculative:
It felt as if her lips had shed
A sigh around her, ere she fled,
Which hung, as on a melting lute,
When all the silver chords are mute,
There lingers still a trembling breath
After the note’s luxurious death,
A shade of song, a spirit air
Of melodies which had been there! (5–12)
S. is known to have admired these Odes (see Mary S.’s letter to Thomas Moore, 18 Janu-
ary 1839, Mary L ii 308). Working from an erratic draft, Mary S. mistook the sequence of
the stanzas, so that earlier eds have printed them in the order 4, 3, 1, 2.
